import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 660

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/660](https://www.erdosproblems.com/660)
- [Er97e] Erdős, Paul, *Some of my favorite problems and results*, The mathematics of Paul Erdős,
  I (1997), 47–67.
- [Al63] Altman, E., *On a problem of P. Erdős*, Amer. Math. Monthly (1963), 148–157.
- [Er75f] Erdős, Paul, *On some problems of elementary and combinatorial geometry*, Ann. Mat. Pura
  Appl. (4) (1975), 99–108.
-/

open scoped EuclideanGeometry

namespace Erdos660

/--
`P` is the set of vertices of a (full-dimensional) convex polyhedron in $\mathbb{R}^3$: the points
are in convex position and they affinely span $\mathbb{R}^3$ (so the polyhedron is genuinely
three-dimensional).
-/
def IsPolyhedronVertices (P : Finset ℝ³) : Prop :=
  ConvexIndependent ℝ ((↑) : ↥(P : Set ℝ³) → ℝ³) ∧ affineSpan ℝ (P : Set ℝ³) = ⊤

/--
Let $x_1, \ldots, x_n \in \mathbb{R}^3$ be the vertices of a convex polyhedron. Are there at least
$$(1 - o(1)) \frac{n}{2}$$
many distinct distances between the $x_i$?

The $(1 - o(1)) \frac{n}{2}$ lower bound is formalised as: for every $\varepsilon > 0$, every set
of $n$ vertices of a convex polyhedron with $n$ sufficiently large determines at least
$(1 - \varepsilon) \frac{n}{2}$ distinct distances.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51 52]
theorem erdos_660 :
    answer(sorry) ↔
      ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, ∀ P : Finset ℝ³,
        P.card = n → IsPolyhedronVertices P →
        (1 - ε) * ((n : ℝ) / 2) ≤ (distinctDistances P : ℝ) := by
  sorry

/--
For the similar problem in $\mathbb{R}^2$ there are always at least $n/2$ distances, as proved by
Altman [Al63].
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 51 52]
theorem erdos_660.variants.altman_planar (n : ℕ) (P : Finset ℝ²)
    (hcard : P.card = n) (hconv : ConvexIndependent ℝ ((↑) : ↥(P : Set ℝ²) → ℝ²))
    (haff : affineSpan ℝ (P : Set ℝ²) = ⊤) :
    n / 2 ≤ distinctDistances P := by
  sorry

/--
In [Er75f] Erdős claims that Altman proved that the vertices determine $\gg n$ many distinct
distances, but gives no reference.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 51 52]
theorem erdos_660.variants.Er75f :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ c > (0 : ℝ), ∀ᶠ n in Filter.atTop, ∀ P : Finset ℝ³,
      P.card = n → IsPolyhedronVertices P →
      c * n ≤ (distinctDistances P : ℝ) := by
  sorry

end Erdos660

findings.description: The module bibliography identifies [Er97e] as “Some of my favorite problems and results,” The mathematics of Paul Erdős, I (1997), 47–67. This is the work the cited website labels [Er97c], not its [Er97e]. Problem 660 specifically cites [Er97e, p.531]. The mathematical statements are unaffected, but the bibliography misidentifies that reference.
findings.source_evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/660 cites “[Er97e,p.531]”. https://www.erdosproblems.com/bibs/Er97e identifies this as Erdős, “Some of my favourite unsolved problems,” Math. Japon. (1997), 527–537. https://www.erdosproblems.com/bibs/Er97c identifies the 47–67 book chapter currently listed in the file.
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the [Er97e] entry with “Erdős, Paul, Some of my favourite unsolved problems. Math. Japon. (1997), 527–537,” optionally specifying p.531. If the book chapter is also intended as an additional reference, list it separately as [Er97c].

findings.description: The docstring says there are at least n/2 distances, whereas the correctly formalized conclusion uses natural-number division and therefore states the floor bound ⌊n/2⌋. The literal real-valued n/2 bound is false for odd n: an equilateral triangle has three vertices but only one distinct distance. This is a documentation slip, not an error in the Lean theorem.
findings.source_evidence: The linked https://www.erdosproblems.com/93 explicitly states “at least ⌊n/2⌋ distinct distances.” Altman, “On a problem of P. Erdős,” Amer. Math. Monthly 70 (1963), p.148, states in its introduction that the minimum for vertices of a convex polygon is “[n/2]”. Erdős [Er75f], p.100, also gives [n/2] and notes equality for a regular polygon (https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1975-25.pdf).
findings.suggested_fix: Change the planar docstring to say “at least ⌊n/2⌋ distinct distances.” Leave the natural-number inequality unchanged.

reformulations.difference: The source’s uniform (1 − o(1))n/2 lower bound is expressed using a positive ε and eventual quantification over natural-number cardinalities.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: On ℕ, Filter.eventually_atTop is exactly existence of a threshold N followed by a universal quantifier over n ≥ N. Substituting n = P.card gives ∀ ε > 0, ∃ N, ∀ P, N ≤ P.card → IsPolyhedronVertices P → (1 − ε)P.card/2 ≤ distinctDistances P. The threshold is uniform over P, as required by the source’s asymptotic lower bound. The scratch file proves the equivalence between the filter formulation and this explicit uniform ε–N statement.

reformulations.difference: The theorem implements the source’s floor bound through natural-number division rather than an explicit floor operation.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For n ∈ ℕ, natural division n / 2 equals the natural floor of the nonnegative real number (n : ℝ)/2. The scratch file proves, for arbitrary natural n and d, that n / 2 ≤ d ↔ ⌊(n : ℝ)/2⌋₊ ≤ d. Thus the Lean conclusion exactly matches the precise Altman statement, notwithstanding the docstring omission reported separately.

reformulations.difference: The existential linear lower bound uses a weak inequality, whereas the printed assertion in [Er75f, p.101] uses D₃ > cn.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: An eventual weak lower bound D ≥ cn with c > 0 implies the eventual strict bound D > (c/2)n, since n > 0 eventually. The converse follows immediately from strict implying weak inequality. The scratch file proves this equivalence for the same uniformly quantified vertex sets; the choice of weak inequality does not change the claimed linear lower bound.

review.notes: All four declarations were checked. The main theorem follows the interpretation explicitly adopted in Thomas Bloom’s October 2025 mathematical discussion; the original wording is acknowledged there as ambiguous. The current source records the main problem as open and the planar result as proved. Its unreferenced attribution of the spatial linear bound to Altman does not establish a status correction. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles without errors and verifies the equivalences above, empty/singleton/two-point distance counts, exclusion of zero distances, the no-point-in-the-hull-of-the-others criterion, the requirement of at least four polyhedron vertices, and existence of an admissible four-vertex set. Full access to the Math. Japon. article and the subscription book chapter was unavailable; the current problem statement, quoted original wording, bibliography records, Altman’s introduction, and the relevant section of Er75f were checked. The target file’s hash still matches the committed version.
